A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, title, and central experiments. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer and Mamba path-finding results, embedding analyses, and experiments on supervision and training dynamics in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds memorization-speed experiments, learning-rate analyses, and weight-tying ablations.

M1.justification: The underlying edge-memorization and path-finding objectives and basic Transformer, Mamba, and Node2Vec procedures remain. The added architecture variants serve as experimental controls; no new proposed learning or inference method is introduced.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same symbolic coverage: in-context and in-weights path-star tasks, tree-star variants, and tiny path-star, grid, cycle, and irregular graphs. The additions vary models and optimization within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The existing model families and random-chance comparisons remain. v2 adds weight-untied Transformer and Node2Vec counterparts to the tied-model geometry comparisons in Section 4.4 and Appendix D.4.

E3.justification: Appendix B.2.2 substantially revises tiny-model configurations: v1 specifies three layers and width 256 for irregular graphs, whereas v2 specifies one layer throughout, smaller TinyGPT/TinySSM configurations, and width 512 for TinyNN. New experiments introduce full-batch optimization, learning-rate comparisons, and weight-tying controls. These are reported setting changes; Figure 21 still describes a three-layer irregular-graph model, leaving that configuration inconsistent.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of how quickly associative versus geometric memory forms (Figures 7–8), learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 22), embedding-similarity comparisons against adjacency matrices (Figures 23–24), and weight-untying ablations (Figures 10–11 and 33–34). The earlier reverse-edge, pause-token, interleaving, and token-order analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new averages across vertices and training curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The main path-finding accuracies remain, but v2 adds substantial findings: associative recall reaches 100% within two full-batch steps at learning rate 0.1 (Figure 7), while geometric structure takes roughly 200 or more steps at learning rate 0.001 (Figure 8). New heatmaps and untied-model results further expand the evidence. Revised tiny-model settings preclude interpreting their replacement visualizations as matched-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Definitions 2a–2b replace the earlier embedding-based hypotheses with logit-based definitions. Appendix E.3 adds propositions and proofs concerning bipartite weight-tied models, arbitrary-graph weight-untied models, and one-step associative learning; v1 contained only the incidence-vector construction retained as Proposition 5. Appendix F's spectral analysis is largely unchanged.

C1.justification: The central geometric-memory and spectral-bias claims remain. v2 adds the explicit introductory claim that associative storage can be easier to discover than geometric storage, incorporating this into the memorization puzzle. The abstract also strengthens 'not more succinct' to 'more complex.'

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations involving associative-first/geometric-later learning, adjacency factorization, and an SVD-based explanation of weight-untying as bipartite geometric memory. Appendix C.3 newly qualifies that projected visualizations alone cannot establish global information, and Section 1.1 adds hallucinated associations as a possible consequence. The existing symbolic-task and model-scale limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2.2 expands and revises per-model, per-graph specifications and explicitly describes TinyNN without residual connections. New experiment captions disclose full-batch optimization and learning rates, while B.5 adds A100-80GB hardware for the largest batches. Code and data access information does not expand.

R1.justification: Section 5.1 substantially expands positioning through node-representation and factorized-knowledge perspectives, engaging newly cited Huang et al., Saxe et al., and matrix-factorization regularization research. Remark 1 explains why those regularization arguments do not directly resolve the paper's memorization puzzle. This changes the substantive relationship to prior work beyond citation additions.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. The detailed failure analysis moves from Section 2.1.1 to Appendix A.1.1; Section 3 is reorganized around explanations, refutations, and the memorization puzzle; Section 4 gains four explanatory subsections. Related work is also substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual comparison table, boxed open questions, and new dynamics, similarity, and weight-untying figures. Figure 1 and the tiny-graph panels are extensively redrawn with clearer edges and consistent colors. Figures 4–5 are additionally redisplayed as Figures 12–13 in Appendix A; the original hyperparameter table is retained as Table 2.

improvement.justification: The new controls, adjacency-comparison heatmaps, clearer figures, and fuller research positioning strengthen the paper. However, new Proposition 3 in Appendix E.3 incorrectly claims zero similarity between nonadjacent vertices within a partition: its adjacency-vector construction gives positive dot products when they share a neighbor. Appendix B.2.2 also conflicts with Figure 21 about model depth. These added proof and reproducibility problems prevent a confident judgment that the substantial benefits produce a net overall improvement.
